facts.text: Families consult printed television schedules to plan evening viewing.
Cable television offers dozens of channels, including dedicated news and children's programming.
Some households receive television broadcasts through a rooftop antenna.
A family gathers for a favorite weekly program at its scheduled broadcast time.
Local television stations report weather warnings and school closings.
A viewer records a program on videotape to watch after work.
Digital video recorders let some viewers save programs without inserting tapes.
A teenager listens to a portable radio while doing chores outdoors.
Drivers hear traffic reports and weather forecasts on the car radio.
Listeners call local radio stations to request music or enter contests.
Morning radio hosts discuss local happenings between songs and advertisements.
The town newspaper carries obituaries, school sports, advertisements, and meeting notices.
A household receives a thick Sunday newspaper filled with advertising inserts.
Some readers follow national news on newspaper websites instead of waiting for print.
A resident reads community announcements posted on a library bulletin board.
A movie theater posts showtimes outside and sells tickets at the counter.
A teenager checks movie listings in the newspaper before meeting friends.
Video rental shops display rows of films sorted by genre.
Customers return rented films by a deadline to avoid late fees.
Some households receive rented movie discs through the mail.
Music shops sell compact discs in plastic cases with printed cover inserts.
Teenagers make mixed music discs to share with friends.
Portable cassette players remain useful for older recordings early in the decade.
A caller leaves a message on a household answering machine when nobody picks up.
A long-distance caller may use a prepaid telephone card to control costs.
Public payphones remain available at some stores and bus stops.
Later in the decade, some residents watch short videos on websites.
